analysis.one_liner: Repeals ACA coverage mandates and benefit rules, caps Medicaid, and swaps subsidies for a flat tax credit.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the ACA requirements that individuals carry insurance and that large employers offer affordable coverage. It would let insurers sell plans that don't cover required benefits or preventive care at no cost, allow plans with annual payout caps, and raise allowed charges against older enrollees. It would replace income-based ACA subsidies with a flat tax credit of $2,500 per adult and $1,500 per child, create new tax-advantaged 'Roth' health savings accounts, repeal the tax on very high-cost employer plans, and turn federal Medicaid payments into fixed per-person grants to states.
analysis.who_benefits: Younger, healthier enrollees would pay less as insurers gain freedom to charge older adults up to five times more. Higher-income households with expensive employer plans gain from repeal of the 'Cadillac tax.' Employers no longer face the mandate to offer affordable coverage. Banks and insurance companies gain a new market administering Roth HSAs, and health insurers gain both looser benefit rules and tax credits that flow through private plans—including the option for Medicaid enrollees to buy private coverage with federal dollars.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insurers, employers, high earners, HSA managers

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates the ACA individual mandate and the requirement that large employers offer affordable coverage to full-time workers, along with the related reporting paperwork [S2][S3]

Creates an advanceable, refundable health insurance tax credit of $2,500 per covered adult and $1,500 per covered child, usable for premiums or contributions to a health savings account—though only up to the amount actually spent on premiums or account contributions, and reduced for anyone who already gets tax-free employer coverage [S2][S3]
Lets states enroll uninsured residents by default in high-deductible plans (with generic-drug-only pharmacy coverage) unless the person opts out [S2][S3]
Repeals the 'Cadillac tax' on high-cost employer health plans [S2][S3]
Establishes Roth health savings accounts with contribution limits of $5,000 per adult (higher for family coverage and for people 55 or older), indexed to medical inflation [S3]
Gives Medicaid enrollees the option to enroll in a private plan that qualifies for the tax credit instead, with the difference deposited into an HSA [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Older and sicker patients would pay more, since states could allow premiums to vary by age up to five-to-one and insurers could sell stripped-down plans that no longer must cover preventive care at no cost or standard essential benefits. Medicaid beneficiaries would bear the risk of per-person federal caps that grow more slowly than costs. People with large unreimbursed medical bills lose the medical expense deduction. Anyone who lets coverage lapse and later enrolls faces a 20% premium penalty for each year without coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Older, sicker patients and Medicaid beneficiaries

drawbacks.text: Health insurance would no longer be required to cover preventive care at no cost or include the ACA's essential health benefits, and states would have to allow plans with annual benefit caps on their exchanges in order to keep premium subsidies for residents [S2][S3]
People who have gone without coverage for a year or more would pay 20% higher premiums for each consecutive year uninsured, lasting up to three times the length of the coverage gap [S2][S3]

Federal Medicaid payments would become fixed per-beneficiary grants, with a federal match of at most 75%, and states could not use the federal money for adults earning above 100% of the poverty line [S2][S3]
The tax deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses would be eliminated (except long-term care premiums) [S2][S3]
The tax credit is available only for coverage that excludes most abortion care, and people who take the new credit are barred from receiving ACA exchange subsidies instead [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives younger, healthier people and employers lower costs and more choice, but it buys that with weaker protections for people most likely to need care: older adults face five-to-one age rating, stripped-down plans with annual caps become subsidy-eligible, a lapse-in-coverage surcharge replaces the mandate penalty, and Medicaid funding shifts to fixed per-person grants that will fall behind medical inflation. The flat $2,500 credit is worth less than ACA subsidies for low-income older adults and, because it is capped at what you actually spend on premiums or HSA contributions, delivers the most to people who can already afford to fund accounts. The bill is a large transfer of health-system risk from employers and the federal government onto older, sicker, and lower-income patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, one sent it to a health subcommittee two days later, and none of them ever took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Sessions (R-TX) introduced the bill on March 1, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce Committees [S1][S5]
On March 3, 2017, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health; no hearing, markup, or floor vote followed [S5]
Five Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did [S4]
The bill sat without action through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it never advanced, the ACA's coverage mandates, benefit requirements, and Medicaid financing all stayed in place; the insurers, employers, and high earners who would have gained from mandate repeal, benefit deregulation, and the Cadillac-tax repeal got none of it, and no one lost the protections it would have removed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one—the bill expired in committee

for.name: Rep. Pete Sessions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to three committees

against.name: House committee leadership (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce)
against.role: Chairs of the three committees of referral, 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote in two years

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred; all six sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat joined the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill loosens benefit requirements—plans need not cover essential health benefits or free preventive care, and plans with annual payout caps become eligible for subsidies—while new tax credits flow through private plans and Medicaid enrollees could buy private coverage with federal dollars. Insurers gain flexibility and a federal revenue channel, but the flexibility comes at the price of thinner coverage for people who get sick. [S2][S3]

Repeal of the employer mandate, its reporting requirements, and the Cadillac tax cuts employer health costs. Workers lose the federal requirement that their employer coverage be affordable and comprehensive. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Banks and financial firms administering health savings accounts
industries.note: Roth HSAs with limits of $5,000 per adult create a large new market for account trustees, and the tax credit is expressly tied to HSA contributions. Households benefit only to the extent they have cash to fund the accounts. [S3]

industries.industry: Hospitals serving low-income and uninsured patients
industries.note: Capping Medicaid at fixed per-beneficiary grants with a 75% federal-match ceiling would shrink payments over time, and the bill's indigent-care grants equal only 25% of each state's unused tax credits. Hospital losses would surface as tighter charity care and cost-shifting to insured patients. [S2][S3]

industries.industry: Higher-income households with generous employer plans
industries.note: Repealing the Cadillac tax removes a 40% excise tax on the most expensive employer plans, a benefit concentrated in higher-earning households, with the cost showing up as forgone federal revenue. [S2][S3]
